2.37 Ground Water. The major aquifer in the vicinity of Falcon Reservoir is the river alluvium. This water is usually good, but during drought periods, levels decline and water of poorer quality is drawn from deeper sources. The Claiborne and Jackson groups which outcrop near the lake provide fresh to slightly saline water (less than 3,000 parts per million dissolved solids) only in restricted areas.
2.38 Falcon Reservoir Fishery. The fishery in Falcon Reservoir is similar to other South Texas lakes with nongame species predominating. Surveys by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) indicate the nongame species in greatest abundance are gizzard shad, threadfin shad, freshwater drum, Rio Grande perch, and the Cyprinids. Game species present in largest numbers are white bass, bluegill, redear sunfish, and white crappie. As an aid to control the overabundant nongame species and to provide additional fishes to the creel, the TPWD has stocked three exotic species. These are walleye fry and fingerlings (4,450,000), Florida largemouth bass fingerlings (750,000) and striped bass fingerlings (150,000).
2.39 The IBWC cooperates with the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department each spring to hold the reservoir surface elevation as constant as possible during the fish spawning periods. The spawning period occurs first at Falcon Reservoir and is followed by the spawning period at Amistad Reservoir. The IBWC attempts to adjust inflows and outflows during these periods to avoid fluctuations of the reservoir littoral areas. A report by the TPWD (Cooke and Mooney, 1974) referenced the effects of water level stabilization on the reservoir ecosystem.
2.40 Recreation. About 270 miles downstream from Amistad is Falcon Reservoir, formed by the International Boundary and Water Commission's first Dam on the Rio Grande. Completed in 1954, public recreational facilities are provided only at the 572-acre Falcon State Recreational Park.
Amistad-Falcon Systems Operation
2.41 Amistad Reservoir is operated in conjunction with Falcon Reservoir to provide optimum flood control, conservation and regulation of the waters of the Rio Grande. The operation of Amistad and Falcon Reservoirs is in accordance with the 1944 Water Treaty between the United States and Mexico.
2.42 The IBWC continuously computes the volumes of water owned by the US and Mexico in the conservation pool of Amistad Reservoir in accordance with the 1944 Water Treaty. The retention or release of conservation water owned by Mexico is determined by the proper Mexican authorities. The Texas Water Rights Commission determines the retention or release of US-owned conservation water based upon requests from downstream users. For flood control purposes, releases of US and Mexican waters from Amistad Reservoir are made at the minimum practicable rates and, if possible, at rates not exceeding the channel capacity of the Rio Grande between Amistad Dam and Falcon Reservoir. The present channel capacity in this reach of the Rio Grande is approximately 10,000 to 15,000 cfs. It may be necessary to release considerably more than the channel capacity during passage of large floods through Amistad Reservoir. The maximum outflow from Amistad Reservoir during passage of the hypothetical Spillway Design Flood would be approximately 1,543,000 cfs with a maximum reservoir elevation of 1145.12 feet above mean sea level. The IBWC determines all releases from Amistad Reservoir for flood control purposes.
